segments.line: Two days later, Ellie gets a fever. The
hospital is dark. Its
backup generators are dead, like everything else. The
doctors are working by candlelight, the way they did
two hundred years ago.
No medicine is coming. No ambulance.
Just a tired doctor with a candle, telling your mom to keep Ellie cool and give her water.
Your mom makes a decision.
Grandpa's farm is ninety kilometers away. It has
a well with a hand pump, a wood stove, chickens, and a field.
Stay in the city, and the water runs out.
Go, and it's four days on foot, with a sick little sister.
Mo's family is staying. 'It'll come back, ' he says. 'The power has to come back. '
But you know the rule.
It doesn't. You
hug him goodbye. He
gives you his bike lights, out of habit. They don't work. You
take them anyway. You
go back to the man with the bat. He hands over the food he promised, and
something else. A map. A paper map.
Suddenly one of the most valuable things in the world. You
load the old bike trailer with everything that matters. Water. Rice. Blankets. The board game.
Ellie rides in the back, wrapped in a blanket. Mom pulls. You push. And
at sunrise, you walk out of the city, and you don't look back. On
the road, you pass hundreds of people walking the other way, into the city, looking for help that isn't there. That
night, you sleep on the floor of an empty school. The
same kind of building you were so happy to skip, one week ago.
